title: The Ethics of Travel: Who Benefits and Who Bears the Cost?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: I want to begin with a question that I think is rarely asked at travel industry conferences: who benefits from tourism, and who bears the cost? Because the data suggests the answer is often not who we assume.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: Tourism is one of the world's largest industries. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, it accounted for approximately 10% of global GDP and employed around 330 million people. These are remarkable figures. But aggregate statistics conceal enormous variation. In many tourist destinations, particularly in the Global South, the lion's share of tourist spending leaks out of the local economy — flowing instead to international hotel chains, airline companies, and tour operators headquartered in wealthy countries.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: This phenomenon is known as "tourism leakage." Research on all-inclusive resorts in the Caribbean, for example, has found that in some cases up to 80 cents of every dollar spent by a tourist leaves the country before the end of the week. The local community receives the environmental impact — the waste, the water usage, the pressure on infrastructure — while the financial benefits flow elsewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: Alongside leakage, there is the question of cultural commodification — the packaging of local culture for tourist consumption. When a living tradition becomes a performance staged for visitors, something is lost. The dance is real; the ceremony is authentic. But it is now performed on a schedule, for an audience that paid for a ticket, and the meaning has shifted. I am not arguing that cultural exchange is bad — far from it. I am arguing that the terms of exchange matter enormously.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: On the environmental side, the figures are stark. Aviation accounts for around 2.5% of global CO2 emissions — but its total warming impact, including non-CO2 effects, is estimated at roughly three times that. Cruise shipping has a similarly disproportionate environmental footprint. And yet demand for both continues to grow. There is a real tension between the individual's freedom to travel and the collective cost of that travel on the climate.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: I want to be clear that I am not opposed to travel. Travel, at its best, is one of the most effective paths to empathy, understanding, and global citizenship. The problem is not travel itself — it is how travel is structured, who benefits from it, and how the costs are distributed. A carbon levy on aviation, directed towards sustainable development in the Global South, would be a step in the right direction. Community-based tourism models that keep spending within local economies have been demonstrated to work. Certification schemes for responsible tourism operators provide information that can guide consumers.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Osei
dialogue.text: The traveller is not the villain of this story. But the traveller is a participant in a global system, and understanding that system — who it serves, who it costs, what it values — is part of what it means to travel responsibly. I would argue it is part of what it means to be a global citizen.
